messages.subject: Truncation by prescribed distance or % of observations?
parts:
I have 105 observations of a rare species surveyed on line transects carried out in varied woodland habitat. There is one obvious outlier, at 122m from the transect line; the rest of the observations are distributed with a reasonable tail out to 63m (the next largest perpendicular distance).

I want just to remove the 122m obs so...
How can I establish whether truncating at a given distance (120m, 100m, etc.?) or the largest 1% of obs is the most suitable approach?

I feel that this is worth asking since I have tried these options and get very different (although not 'significant') population estimates (ESW's vary between 28.1 and 31.8).

Many thanks in advance for any advice on this.
-Keith.

messages.subject: Re: Truncation by prescribed distance or % of observations?
parts:
> > I have 105 observations of a rare species surveyed on line transects
> > carried out in varied woodland habitat. There is one obvious outlier,
> > at 122m from the transect line; the rest of the observations are
> > distributed with a reasonable tail out to 63m (the next largest
> > perpendicular distance).
> >
> > I want just to remove the 122m obs so...
> > How can I establish whether truncating at a given distance (120m, 100m,
> > etc.?) or the largest 1% of obs is the most suitable approach?
> >
> > I feel that this is worth asking since I have tried these options and
> > get very different (although not 'significant') population estimates
> > (ESW's vary between 28.1 and 31.8).

Keith, if you truncate more, ESW will necessarily reduce, but this doesn't
usually lead to a corresponding increase in the popn abundance estimate
(because encounter rate also reduces as observations are truncated).
However, if you don't truncate sufficiently, odd things can happen if the
model fails to handle the tail of the distribution sensibly. So for your
data, the largest truncation distance I would even consider using would
be the value of your second largest obsn - 63m (or perhaps say 65m). Any
larger value, and you're expecting the model to fit the tail of your
distribution but without any data. Whether it is worth truncating more
than this depends on whether the remaining data exhibit a tail that is
difficult to model.

Steve
